name: Recovery & New Patterns
purpose: Return to relevant dev topics with fresh patterns. Tests recovery after noise. If new learners were created in phase 3, they should absorb relevant data.
items: Refactored entire error handling. Replaced try/catch with Result<T, E> type. Functions return Success or Failure explicitly. No more invisible throw chains.
Event sourcing prototype complete. Every state change is an immutable event. Current state = fold over event stream. Replay is trivial. Mindset shift from 'state' to 'facts'.
CI migration from Jenkins to GitHub Actions. YAML syntax is cleaner, marketplace has pre-built actions, no server to maintain. Migration took 2 days.
Navigator-driver pairing only works if the navigator navigates. In practice they zone out after 15 minutes. Switching roles every 10 minutes keeps both engaged.
Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry. Every request gets a trace ID across services. Checkout 800ms = 200ms auth + 150ms inventory + 400ms payment + 50ms response.
Strangler fig pattern for decomposing the payment monolith. New flows go through new service, old flows stay. Gradual migration, zero big-bang risk.
Anomaly detection with isolation forests on API access patterns. No labeled data needed. Caught 3 suspicious patterns in the first week.
UX team redesigned onboarding with progressive disclosure. 3 essential settings first, rest discoverable. Completion rate: 34% → 78%.
Automated canary analysis with Kayenta. Statistical comparison between canary and baseline. No more subjective 'looks good to me' decisions.
Design docs before coding slowed us 20% per feature but eliminated 3 mid-sprint pivots that would have cost 200%+ each. Upfront investment pays.
CAP theorem in practice. AP by default with optional CP for critical paths like payments. Per-feature choice rather than system-wide.
Trunk-based development with feature flags. No merge conflicts, code ships daily behind flags. Release = flip a flag. Decoupled from deployment.
Senior dev mentors by questions: 'What would happen if...' 'Why did you choose...' 'What's the tradeoff...' Slower but juniors learn to reason independently.
Containerized ML pipeline. Training on GPU containers, inference on CPU with auto-scaling. Reproducible environments fixed 'works on my machine' for models.
6-month reflection: proudest decisions were choosing NOT to build. No microservices, no Kubernetes, no custom auth. Simplicity is a feature.
Implemented CQRS for our reporting system. Write path is simple CRUD, read path is optimized materialized views. Reads went from 3 seconds to 50ms.

Added property-based testing for our data transformation functions. Instead of testing specific inputs, generate random valid inputs and assert invariants hold. Found 4 edge cases conventional tests missed.
Implemented saga pattern for distributed transactions. If the payment succeeds but shipping fails, the saga compensates by refunding the payment. No distributed locks needed.
Migrated from polling to server-sent events for real-time dashboard updates. Reduced API calls by 95%. Each client holds one persistent connection instead of hitting the endpoint every 5 seconds.
Built a custom linter rule that prevents importing from internal module paths. Forces teams to use public APIs. Caught 12 violations that would have broken during the next refactor.
Implemented backpressure in our event processing pipeline. When the consumer falls behind, it signals the producer to slow down. Prevents memory exhaustion during traffic spikes.

Zero-downtime database migrations using the expand-contract pattern. Step 1: add new column. Step 2: dual-write. Step 3: backfill. Step 4: swap reads. Step 5: drop old column. Each step is independently deployable.
Added a 'debug mode' to our API that includes timing breakdowns in response headers. X-Server-Timing: db=12ms, cache=2ms, auth=5ms, render=8ms. Frontend team loves it for performance debugging.

Implemented a circuit breaker dashboard. Visual indicator of which external services are healthy (green), degraded (yellow), or tripped (red). The dashboard is the first thing we check during incidents.
Switched from UUID v4 to ULID for primary keys. Sortable by creation time, shorter, URL-safe, and doesn't fragment B-tree indexes like random UUIDs do.
Built observability into our feature flags. Every flag evaluation is logged with context (user, environment, result). Can answer 'who saw what version when' instantly.
Implemented read-your-writes consistency for our eventually-consistent system. After a write, the user's subsequent reads are routed to the primary. Other users hit replicas. Best of both worlds.
Added flamegraph generation to our profiling toolkit. One command generates a flamegraph from production traffic. Immediately saw that 40% of CPU time was in JSON serialization.
Implemented idempotent API endpoints using idempotency keys stored in Redis with a 24-hour TTL. Retry-safe by default. Duplicate requests return the cached response.
Our monitoring evolved: started with uptime checks, added APM traces, then custom business metrics, then anomaly detection. Each layer catches different categories of issues.
Implemented database row-level security with PostgreSQL RLS policies. Instead of filtering in application code, the database itself enforces tenant isolation. Defense in depth.
Built a migration verification tool. After each DB migration, it runs a set of invariant checks: no orphaned records, foreign keys valid, indexes not bloated. Catches data corruption early.
Adopted the 'boring architecture' manifesto. Our stack: PostgreSQL, Redis, Node.js, React. Nothing exotic. Every engineer on the team can debug any component. Expertise is shared.
Implemented graceful degradation for our search feature. If Elasticsearch is down, fall back to PostgreSQL full-text search. Slower but functional. Users notice degradation, not failure.

Added structured concurrency to our async operations. Instead of fire-and-forget promises, all async work is tied to a scope. When a request ends, all its child tasks are cleaned up. No more orphaned background work.
Created a production debug toolkit: feature flag overrides per-user, request replay from logs, time-travel queries on the event store. Debugging production issues without ssh-ing into servers.

Implemented webhook fan-out with ordered delivery guarantee. Events are partitioned by entity ID, each partition processed in order. Out-of-order delivery was causing cascading bugs in downstream systems.

Our test strategy crystallized into three layers: fast unit tests (milliseconds, run on save), integration tests (seconds, run on commit), end-to-end tests (minutes, run on merge). Each layer catches different bug categories.
Added automatic API changelog generation from OpenAPI spec diffs. Every deploy produces a human-readable list of changes. Consumers know exactly what changed without reading code.
Implemented a cost-per-request calculator. Each API endpoint shows its compute, database, and third-party API costs. Found one endpoint costing $0.02 per call — 100x more than average. Optimized it.

Built a deployment confidence score. Combines: test coverage of changed files, number of files changed, whether it touches critical paths, time since last deploy. Score below 70% requires manual approval.
Implemented progressive rollouts with automatic rollback. If error rate increases by >2% during rollout, it automatically rolls back and pages the on-call engineer. Caught a bad deploy at 5% rollout.
Our API now supports field-level permissions. Different API key scopes can read/write different fields of the same resource. No more all-or-nothing access. Required for SOC 2 compliance.
Created a dependency injection container that's just a TypeScript Map with type inference. 30 lines of code, zero dependencies, full compile-time safety. Sometimes the simplest solution is the best.
Implemented chaos testing for our cache layer. Randomly returns cache misses for 1% of requests in staging. Ensures the system gracefully falls back to source-of-truth on cache failures.

Our deploy pipeline now includes a database query plan analysis step. If any migration causes a sequential scan on a table with >1M rows, the pipeline fails. Prevents accidental performance regressions.

Built a lightweight service catalog. Each service has: owner, dependencies, SLO, runbook link, and on-call schedule. One page per service. No fancy tooling — just a markdown file per service in a shared repo.

Added automatic PR labeling based on changed file paths. Changes in /api/ get 'backend' label, /components/ gets 'frontend', /migrations/ gets 'database'. Routes PRs to the right reviewers automatically.

Implemented request coalescing for our most expensive endpoint. If 50 identical requests come in within 100ms, we execute the query once and share the result. Reduced DB load by 80% during peak traffic.
Our final architecture insight this quarter: the best systems aren't the ones with the most features — they're the ones where every engineer can hold the entire design in their head.
